title: Bread from Heaven
sum: The long retelling of the Exodus goes on. Three more pairs set Egypt beside Israel. Vermin took away Egypt's appetite, while Israel got quail (16:1–4). Snakes bit Israel in the wilderness, but the bronze snake was a token of salvation, and it was God, "the Savior of all," who healed them, not the thing they looked at (16:5–14). Hail with fire inside it destroyed Egypt's crops, while the manna, "the food of angels," fed Israel (16:15–29).

The chapter's theology is bold: creation serves its Maker. Fire burns in water to punish, and fire forgets its power to spare the ice-like manna. The manna even tasted like whatever each person wanted. The lesson is Deuteronomy's: people do not live by crops alone, but God's word keeps them. And because the manna melted at sunrise, the writer draws a rule for prayer: thank God before the sun is up.
readings: Read as a sermon on Exodus and Numbers

The writer does not tell the story in order. He picks scenes from Exodus 9, 16 and Numbers 11 and 21 and sets them in pairs to show one truth: what punished Egypt helped Israel. He leaves out Israel's grumbling and stresses God's mercy.
Read with John 6 and the Eucharist

John 6 invites a reading of 16:20–29 beside it: there the crowd quotes "Bread from heaven he gave them to eat" (John 6:31) and Jesus calls himself the true bread. Albert the Great quotes 16:20 for the food of the Eucharist, and a processional of 1537 sets its words as the versicle and response of the Corpus Christi procession. The writer himself speaks of the manna.

views.C: The Catholic Church reads Wisdom as Scripture. Its Latin liturgy of the Eucharist took a versicle and response from 16:20, "You provided them bread from heaven" / "having every delight within it" (the site's rendering; a processional of 1537 gives them for the Corpus Christi procession), and Albert the Great quotes the verse for the food of the Eucharist beside John 6:54.
views.P: For the Church of England, Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles lists "the Book of Wisdom" among the books the Church reads "for example of life and instruction of manners" but does not use to establish doctrine. Read that way, the chapter's teaching that healing and food come from God's word, not from objects, stands close to John 3:14–15 (16:7) and to Deuteronomy 8:3 and Matthew 4:4 (16:26).
views.H: The chapter uses Greek learning: musical language for creation (16:20, 24), and a retelling of the manna that later rabbis shared (the manna's many tastes, Yoma 75a). The pairing of plagues and blessings is a deliberate literary scheme.
views.J: Later rabbinic texts make the same points: the bronze snake did not heal by itself (Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 3:8), and the manna tasted of all kinds of food (Yoma 75a). The book itself was not kept in the Jewish canon.

deep.b: Chapters 11–19 are built on a pattern that the book states in 11:5: "The very things that punished their enemies / were the things that did them good when they were in need." Readers usually count seven pairs: water from the rock against the Nile turned to blood (11:1–14); quail against vermin (16:1–4); healing against deadly bites (16:5–14); manna against hail (16:15–29); light against darkness (17:1–18:4); the firstborn spared against the firstborn struck (18:5–25); the sea crossed against the sea that drowned (19:1–9). Chapter 16 holds three of the seven. The scheme is not history in order but a meditation: one event shown from two sides.

deep.h: The manna in Wisdom, the rabbis and the church
deep.b: Wisdom adds four things to Exodus and Numbers. The manna is "the food of angels" (from the Greek Psalm 77:25). It tasted of whatever the eater wanted (16:20–21). It stood up to fire yet melted in the sun, which shows the elements obeying God (16:22–23, 27). And its lesson is that God's word, not the harvest, keeps people alive (16:26). The Talmud keeps the first two ideas, with a debate about whether angels eat at all (Yoma 75a–b). John 6 and 1 Corinthians 10:3 take the manna as pointing to Christ. The Latin liturgy of Corpus Christi sings Wisdom's line as a versicle and response.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the dawn lesson answers the quail
deep.b: The chapter opens with craving (16:2–3) and closes with gratitude (16:28–29). I suggest the order is deliberate: the wilderness story of Numbers 11, where craving for quail ended in death, is answered by a habit of thanks at dawn, before any food is gathered. The "ungrateful" whose hope melts like frost (16:29) are the opposite of the people who rise before the sun to thank God. The dawn-prayer lesson is stated in 16:28 itself; the link back to the craving of 16:2 is my own reading.

title: A Night No Fire Could Light
sum: The fifth contrast begins: the plague of darkness. Exodus gives it three verses; Wisdom gives it a whole chapter. The Egyptians who thought they could hold a holy nation down lie imprisoned by a long night. No fire or star can light it. Phantoms appear, noises terrify them, and the magicians who sold cures for fear are the most afraid of all.

In the middle of the story the writer stops to analyze fear: wickedness is a coward, gripped by conscience, and fear is the betrayal of reason's help. The darkness is inside them as much as outside. Every sound of nature, wind, birdsong, water, an echo, turns to terror. Meanwhile the whole rest of the world goes about its work in light. The night is "a picture of the darkness that was going to take them in," and the Egyptians are "a heavier weight to themselves than the darkness."
readings: The chapter is a study of a guilty mind. It uses Greek moral language (conscience, reason, fear) to explain how sin turns harmless things into threats.
Read as a picture of judgment

The darkness is a foretaste of the final darkness (17:21), the opposite of the light that God's holy ones enjoy (18:1). Compare Jesus' words on "the darkness outside" (Matthew 8:12) and the "gloom of darkness" in Jude 1:13.

views.H: The chapter is the work of a Greek-trained author: the definition of fear (17:12), the word for conscience (its first moral use in the Greek Bible), and a catalog of natural sounds. It expands Exodus 10:21–23 with an eye on Egyptian magic.
views.J: Later Jewish commentary also enlarged the darkness plague. Rashi on Exodus 10:22, citing Midrash Tanchuma and Exodus Rabbah 14:3, says it came in two spells of three days, the second so thick that no one sitting could stand up, and that wicked Israelites who did not want to leave Egypt died during it. Wisdom's chapter is a much earlier example of reading the plague closely.

deep.b: Wisdom 17:11–13 is a short essay inside the story. The guilty imagine the worst because their conscience accuses them; fear is reason giving up; and not knowing the cause is worse than the cause. The word συνείδησις, "conscience," occurs in Swete's Greek Old Testament only here and in Ecclesiastes 10:20, where it means private thought. So this is the first place in the Greek Bible where conscience accuses. Paul will use the word often (Romans 2:15; 1 Corinthians 8:7). The writer's point is moral, not only psychological: the Egyptians' torment came from within because their sin was "secret" (17:3) and their minds were "undisciplined" (17:1).

echoes: Exodus 10:21–23; Exodus 7:11; Exodus 8:18–19; 2 Timothy 3:8; Romans 2:15; Matthew 8:12; Jude 1:6; Jude 1:13; 2 Peter 2:4; John 1:5

title: The All-Powerful Word
sum: Israel had light while Egypt sat in darkness, and the pillar of fire led them out (18:1–4). Then the sixth contrast: the night of the firstborn. Egypt had planned to kill Israel's babies; one child, Moses, was put out to die and saved. Now Egypt's own children die, and its army will drown. Israel, forewarned, keeps the first Passover in secret, already singing praise, while from Egypt comes a cry all out of tune (18:5–13).

At midnight, in deep silence, God's all-powerful word leaps from heaven like a warrior with a sharp sword, filling everything with death, reaching to heaven yet standing on earth (18:14–16). The chapter ends with the one time death touched Israel in the wilderness, the plague after Korah's rebellion. A blameless man, Aaron, ran into the crowd with prayer and incense, stood between the dead and the living, and turned the destroyer back, wearing on his robe the whole world (18:20–25).
readings: The chapter is the book's Passover: the night foretold to the fathers, the secret sacrifice, the shared vow, the hymns, the death of the firstborn, and Israel confessed as God's son (Exodus 4:22). The Catholic Lectionary reads 18:6–9 on a Sunday with Hebrews 11, which praises the faith of Abraham.

The Roman Rite sang 18:14–15 in the Christmas season, as the Introit of the Sunday within the octave of Christmas in a Missal of about 1476 and as an antiphon in the Roman Breviary: "While all things held the middle of silence ... your all-powerful word, Lord, came from the royal thrones" (the site's rendering of the Latin). In context the word comes to judge Egypt; the liturgy reads the descent of the word in the light of John 1:14, the Word made flesh.

views.C: The Roman Rite sang 18:14–15 in the Christmas season (Dum medium silentium), reading the word leaping from heaven as a figure of the Incarnation, and the Lectionary for Mass reads 18:6–9 on the Nineteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time, Year C, with Hebrews 11.
views.H: The word is a personification of God's judgment, like the destroyer of Exodus 12:23 and the destroying angel of 1 Chronicles 21:15–16, and the cosmic robe matches Philo and Josephus. Wisdom was written before John's Gospel; both draw on the Jewish picture of God's word.
views.J: The chapter's Passover has the night of watching (Exodus 12:42) and hymns of praise, as the Mishnah later sets the Hallel at the Passover meal (Mishnah Pesachim 10:6). The cosmic meaning of the high priest's robe is shared with Philo and Josephus.

deep.b: Exodus says the LORD himself struck the firstborn (Exodus 12:29), yet also speaks of "the destroyer" (Exodus 12:23). Wisdom brings these together in one figure: God's "all-powerful word" comes down from the royal thrones as a warrior with a sword (18:15–16). The figure draws on the angel of 1 Chronicles 21:16, "standing between earth and sky, his sword drawn," and on the song "The LORD is a man of war" (Exodus 15:3). The word acts for God without being separate from him, and later in the chapter God's anger is called "the punisher" and "the destroyer" (18:22, 25). Read in its own setting it is a powerful personification, in the same family as Wisdom herself in chapters 7–10. The Christmas liturgy sings it of Christ, and it reads naturally beside John 1:1–14 and Revelation 19:13–15.

The last scene adds what Numbers 16 does not say: Aaron won "with a word," reminding God of the oaths to the fathers, and his robe carried "the whole world" (18:22–24). Philo of Alexandria, who may have been close in time and place to the writer, says the high priest's robe is "a copy and representation of the world," so that the whole world enters with him when he prays (Life of Moses 2.117, 133). Josephus explains the parts of the dress as earth, sky, the ocean, the sun and moon, and the months or the signs of the zodiac (Antiquities 3.179–187). For Wisdom the point is that the priest stands for all creation before God, and that creation itself, worn on the robe, turned back the plague.

deep.title: Claude's theory: two figures between heaven and earth
deep.b: Chapter 18 has two figures who stand "between." The word stands on earth and reaches heaven, filling everything with death (18:16). Aaron stands between the dead and the living and stops death (18:23). I suggest the writer means them as a matched pair: the same God who sends the destroying word also gives the priest whose word stops it, and in both cases a "word" (λόγος, 18:15 and 18:22) does the work. Each scene is plain in the text; the deliberate pairing is my own reading.

title: Creation Made New
sum: The seventh and last contrast: the sea. The Egyptians, still burying their dead, change their minds and chase the people they had begged to leave, dragged on by the fate they deserved. For Israel the whole creation is reshaped from the start: the cloud shades the camp, dry land rises from the water, a clear road runs through the Red Sea, and a green plain appears where the waves had been. The people leap like lambs and praise their rescuer (19:1–9).

Remembering Egypt, they recall creation turned upside down: gnats from the ground, frogs from the river; and in the wilderness, a new kind of birth for birds, the quail from the sea (19:10–12). Egypt is judged worse than Sodom: Sodom turned strangers away, but Egypt welcomed Jacob's family and then enslaved them (19:13–17). The book ends by explaining the miracles: the elements were re-tuned like the strings of a harp (19:18–21), and with one line of praise: God has stood by his people "at every time and in every place."
readings: The crossing of the sea is a second creation. Dry land rises out of water as on the third day (Genesis 1:9–10), each creature acts "in its own kind" (Genesis 1:21–25), and the elements change roles at God's command. Compare Isaiah's "something new" on the road through the sea (Isaiah 43:16–19), with Paul's "new creation" (2 Corinthians 5:17) and with the new heaven and earth (Revelation 21:1).
Read as a word to Alexandria

The comparison with Sodom (19:13–17) is aimed at Egypt's treatment of guests who had "shared the same rights." Jews in Alexandria, who in Philo's account were attacked under the prefect Flaccus and called "foreigners and aliens" (Against Flaccus 54), could hear their own story in it, and the closing promise that God stands by his people "in every place."

views.H: 19:18–21 explains miracles in Greek terms: the elements re-ordered, not abolished. The Sodom comparison and the language of rights under law (19:16) are clues to a setting among Jews in Egypt.
views.J: The ending, God's presence with Israel "at every time and in every place," speaks to a people living away from the land, as the Jews of Egypt were, and the joy of 19:9 recalls the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15).

deep.b: Wisdom 19:18 gives one of the earliest Jewish explanations of how miracles work. The elements, earth, water, air and fire, are like the strings of a harp. Played another way, the same strings make a new pattern "and yet keep their own sound." So in the Exodus land animals walked through water, frogs came onto land, fire burned in water, and fire did not melt the ice-like manna (19:19–21; 16:17–23). God does not break the world to save his people; he plays it differently. The idea draws on Greek science while keeping the biblical God in control, and it ties together the whole book's view of a creation that "fights for the righteous" (16:17; 5:17–20).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the book ends on a chord
deep.b: Musical words gather in the last chapters: the manna "in tune with every taste" (16:20), creation "tightening" and "slackening" like a string (16:24), Israel's songs of praise against Egypt's out-of-tune cry (18:9–10), and the elements re-tuned like a harp (19:18). I suggest the writer means the Exodus to be heard as music that God plays on creation, so that the last verse, praise at every time and place, is the final chord rather than an unfinished ending. The harp image is the book's own (19:18); reading the earlier musical words as one design is my own proposal.

views: 19:13–17 can be heard as a protest against the treatment of Jews in Egypt, such as the attacks under the prefect Flaccus that Philo describes (Against Flaccus).
The comparison can also be read as general: hospitality to strangers is the test of a nation, and God judges its betrayal.
